beats.narration_text: Hello, I'm Vineet S.. A chatbot answers. An A I agent acts. It can look things up, call your systems, and work through a task in many steps. That changes what a product manager has to design. Here is what to know.

props.command: What is an AI agent, and how is it different from a chatbot?
output: An agent acts, it does not only answer
It calls tools and APIs in a loop
Memory and limits make it safe to use

beats.narration_text: An AI agent is a model that plans, then uses tools and acts. A chatbot replies once. An agent decides what to do next, does it, checks the result, and keeps going until the job is done.

props.text:
An AI agent is
just a chatbot
with a longer answer.

props.replacementWords: a model that plans, then uses tools and acts

beats.narration_text: Here are the five ideas. Tools and APIs. Tool calling. Multi-step reasoning. Memory. And agentic products. Together they turn a model that talks into a system that gets work done.

A tool is a function the agent is allowed to use, like search, a calendar, a database or a payment API. In tool calling, the model does not run the tool itself. It writes a structured request, your system runs it, and the result goes back to the model. So you decide exactly what the agent can touch.

layers.title: Your system runs it
layers.sub: You control what the agent can touch

layers.title: The result returns
layers.sub: The model reads it and decides next

beats.narration_text: Here is the loop. The goal and the available tools go to the agent. It plans a step, calls a tool, reads what came back, and decides what to do next. It repeats until the task is done or it needs help. For example, an agent booking travel might search flights, compare prices, then ask you to confirm.

Multi-step reasoning is what lets an agent break a big goal into small steps and adjust when a step fails. Memory is what lets it keep going. Short-term memory holds the current task. Long-term memory stores preferences and past results. But every error can compound across steps, so more steps means more risk.

layers.title: Multi-step reasoning
layers.sub: Break a goal into steps, adapt on failure

layers.title: Short-term memory
layers.sub: The task so far, in the context window

layers.title: Errors compound
layers.sub: More steps means more chances to go wrong

beats.narration_text: Agentic products are already everywhere. A coding assistant that edits files and runs tests. A support agent that looks up an order and issues a refund. A research assistant that searches, reads and writes a report. And a scheduling assistant that coordinates calendars. Each one uses tools, steps and memory.

What do product managers decide? First, which tools the agent may use, and with what permissions. Second, where a human must approve, especially for money or deleting data. Third, how you measure success across a whole task, not one answer. And fourth, a step limit and a cost limit, so a loop cannot run away.

layers.title: Tools and permissions
layers.sub: What it may touch, and how much

layers.title: Task-level success
layers.sub: Measure the whole job, not one reply

layers.title: Step and cost limits
layers.sub: So a loop cannot run away

beats.narration_text: So, agents. They plan, call tools, and act in a loop. Memory carries the task. And you design the permissions, the approvals and the limits.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. I am a product manager considering an AI agent for this job: [describe it]. List the tools it would need, the steps it would take, what it should remember, and which actions need human approval. Then describe the three most likely ways it could fail across multiple steps, and the limits I should set. The failure modes are the valuable part. Agents rarely fail on step one, they fail on step six after an early mistake, so write a test for each failure Claude lists. Pause here and run it on your own product.
